messages.subject: Moderation
messages.body_plain:
Hi Everyone,

I have a query, would be great if someone can advise me on this. I am trying to run a moderation effect using the code below:

model27<-'PowerT=~DP3+DP4+DP5
ObT=~DOR2+DOR3+DOR5
KnowT=~DK1+DK2+DK3+DK4
DO=~PowerT+ObT+KnowT
DK3~~DK4
BMS=~BMS1+BMS2+BMS3_REV+BMS4+
BMS5_REV+BMS6+BMS7+BMS8
WFC=~WFC1+WFC2+WFC3+WFC4+WFC5
RCW=~RCW1+RCW2+RCW3+RCW4
WFE=~WFE1+WFE2+WFE3
PC=~PC1+PC2+PC3
GRE=~GRE1+GRE2+GRE3+GRE4
WFCust=~WFCust1+WFCust2+WFCust3+WFCust4
IntGRERCW=~GRE*RCW
IntDOPCWFCust=~DO*PC*WFCust
WFC~DO
WFE~DO
WFC~IntGRERCW
WFE~IntGRERCW
WFC~BMS
WFE~BMS
WFC~IntDOPCWFCust
WFE~IntDOPCWFCust'

The output is not generating regressions for the red highlighted part and continues to give output of the previous code. (Interaction of PC*WFCust). Here is the output that was generated :

Regressions:
                   Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)   Std.lv  Std.all
  WFC ~
    DO               -0.223    0.258   -0.862    0.389   -0.045   -0.045
  WFE ~
    DO                0.290    0.196    1.477    0.140    0.079    0.079
  WFC ~
    IntGRERCW         0.056    0.072    0.787    0.431    0.037    0.037
  WFE ~
    IntGRERCW         0.632    0.060   10.528    0.000    0.563    0.563
  WFC ~
    BMS               0.244    0.082    2.993    0.003    0.121    0.121
  WFE ~
    BMS               0.181    0.058    3.098    0.002    0.120    0.120
  WFC ~
    IntPCWFCust       0.557    0.045   12.460    0.000    0.616    0.616
  WFE ~
    IntPCWFCust      -0.015    0.023   -0.667    0.505   -0.023   -0.023

It also reported an error before it generated output (the code works despite the error).  It is this :

Error in lavaanify(model = FLAT, constraints = constraints, varTable = lavdata@ov,  :
  lavaan ERROR: wrong number of arguments in modifier (DO,PC) of element IntDOPCWFCust=~WFCust

Can someone help me understand the error and what can be done in this case. Your help is appreciated.

Regards
Mahima

messages.subject: Re: Moderation
messages.body_plain:
Lavaan in its current version doesn't have support for latent interaction moderation yet. You need to estimate the interaction manually and specify it as a variable in the model.

Regards,

Nikos

messages.subject: Re: What should I do if I would like lavaan to return me a matrix with missing values filled by FIML?
messages.subject_clean: What should I do if I would like lavaan to return me a matrix with missing values filled by FIML?
messages.body_plain:
FIML does not replace missing values. That replacement is called "imputation," and you can use the imputation tools in the semTools package if that is what you want. FIML optimizes an overall likelihood within the context of the missing observations and the free parameters, but it does not supply a set of replacement values for the missing observations.

messages.subject: Re: Moderation
messages.body_plain:
Mahima,

Are you sure that you are looking at output generated by the most recent estimation attempt?  When debugging situations like this, I sometimes find it helpful to adopt the following defensive programming idiom.

myModel <- '....'
rm(myFit)
myFit <- lavaan(myModel, ...)
summary(myFit)

That way, you either get output from the most recent estimation attempt or none at all.

Keith

messages.subject: Re: Moderation
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mahima,

The issue in your code is that you're trying to estimate interactions between latent variables within the syntax. lavaan does not (currently, as far as I know) have this capability (you can estimate interactions for observed predictors, just not latent variables). If you're interested in interactions among latent variables you have two choices the LMS/QML method (implemented in Mplus and the package nlsem) or product indicator approaches (see the indProd function in semTools for details).

Alex

messages.subject: Re: Moderation
messages.body_plain:
I don't think the two way interactions were working either :(. In lavaan syntax a star, *, cannot be used to specify an interaction between variables. Instead a * is used to create a label for a parameter. So for your two way interactions you were creating a new variable the was equivalent to one of the indicators with a label that was the name of the other indicator.

messages.subject: Correcting for Measurement Error in Path Models
messages.subject_clean: Correcting for Measurement Error in Path Models
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I am somewhat new to lavaan, and trying to determine the appropriate way to apply Bollen's (1989) (1-alpha)*(variance) correction for measurement error within a path model using lavaan. I am using lavaan to run an Actor-Partner Interdependence Model path analysis (Kenny, Kashy, & Cook, 2006). My predictors are single items, and my outcomes are composites based on multi-item scales; the outcomes are the ones I am applying the error corrections to. I am using path analysis due to my relatively small sample size (75 dyads). I initially ran the following model to apply the measurement error corrections in my analysis:

#

# Approach 1 - applying error correction directly to the observed composite

#

library(lavaan);

modelData <-read.csv(file=..., header = TRUE);

model<-"

DVmale ~ X1male + X2male + X1female + X2female

DVfemale ~ X1female+ X2female + X1male + X2male

DVmale ~~ 0.1528028*DVmale

DVfemale ~~ 0.2171088*DVfemale

DVmale ~~ DVfemale

";

result<-sem(model, data=modelData, estimator = "ML", fixed.x=FALSE, missing = "FIML");

summary(result, fit.measures=TRUE, standardized=TRUE)

When I run the model using Approach 1, most of the regression paths are significant and in the theoretically predicted direction. However, the model fit is very poor - in fact, unrealistically so (RMSEA > 2, CFI = 0, Chi-square/df ratio > 400, etc.). Although there is evidence that model fit statistics can be quite inappropriately biased toward model rejection when degrees of freedom and sample size are low (Kenny, Kaniskan, & McCoach, 2015), as they were in this study (n = 75, df = 2), these fit measures seem so off-base to me that I am concerned about the results as a whole. If I were not applying error corrections at all, I would have fully saturated model, and therefore (trivially) perfect fit. But the addition of the error corrections is adding 2 df to the model, putting me in a small-df situation for estimating model fit. Following Kenny (http://davidakenny.net/kkc/c7/c7.htm), I am essentially using the APIM as a "regression hack" to account for the fact that scores for male and female members of couples are non-independent - model fit per se is not my primary concern, but rather the significance and direction of the regression coefficients. That said, I began to wonder if perhaps I was incorrectly applying the error correction. So I tried the approach below, which explicitly models the outcomes as latent variables with single indicators.

#

# Approach 2 - Applying error correction to single indicators of latent outcome variables

#

library(lavaan);

modelData <-read.csv(file=..., header = TRUE);

model<-"

DVmale_Latent =~ 1.0*DVmale_Observed

DVfemale_Latent =~ 1.0*DVfemale_Observed

DVmale_Latent ~ X1male + X2male + X1female + X2female

DVfemale_Latent ~ X1female + X2female + X1male + X2male

DVmale_Observed ~~ .13106046*DVmale_Observed

DVfemale_Observed ~~ .1571883984*DVfemale_Observed

DVmaleLatent ~~ DVfemaleLatent

";

result<-sem(model, data=modelData, estimator = "ML", fixed.x=FALSE, missing = "FIML");

summary(result, fit.measures=TRUE, standardized=TRUE)

With Approach 2 above, I get a saturated model and the fit issue resolves (at least, in the sense of a saturated model fitting "perfectly"). But now none of the regression paths are significant. Although I have read a good bit about error corrections in SEM, I am a bit confused whether I am applying them appropriately in lavaan, as well as the more general question of which of the two approaches above is correct (or maybe neither of them)? I'd appreciate any insights.

messages.subject: Re: Correcting for Measurement Error in Path Models
messages.subject_clean: Correcting for Measurement Error in Path Models
messages.body_plain:
OK, I'm embarrassed--this took me wayyyy too long to figure out.
     In model 1, you are conflating "measurement error" (as it is simplistically understood) with "structural error," the variance in the dependents not accounted for by the predictors. In model 1, you are constraining R2 for the two dependents, and that is your problem. You are forcing your predictors to explain a specific fraction of the dependents' total variance, and the predictors are not doing that. Hence the lack of fit.
     In model 2, you are separating what is called "measurement error" from "structural error." In model 2, the factors have "structural errors," and those are free to vary, depending on the predictive success of the predictors. The two dependent observed variables have their "measurement errors" constrained, which is what (I think) you intended. You can't achieve this result (through this kind of modeling) without creating the factors. The constraints on the "measurement errors" do not affect fit because those parameters would not be identified anyway--they have to be fixed to some values, and it would be hard to find values such that the chi-square and other fit indices will complain about them. (Try it--double or triple your values and see what happens.)
     You *could* achieve the same thing by running the model without constraints but then adjusting all results for the reliability estimates, but since you have a method that does the job, who needs another one?
     Your model 1 gains 2 DF and poor fit because you are constraining the structural errors for the dependents. Your model 2 has 0 DF because the two structural errors are free to conform to the data.

Hi,

> On 4 Aug 2017, at 24:16 , Tim <worl...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi,
> I am somewhat new to lavaan, and trying to determine the appropriate way to apply Bollen's (1989) (1-alpha)*(variance) correction for measurement error within a path model using lavaan. I am using lavaan to run an Actor-Partner Interdependence Model path analysis (Kenny, Kashy, & Cook, 2006). My predictors are single items, and my outcomes are composites based on multi-item scales; the outcomes are the ones I am applying the error corrections to. I am using path analysis due to my relatively small sample size (75 dyads). I initially ran the following model to apply the measurement error corrections in my analysis:
>
> #
> # Approach 1 - applying error correction directly to the observed composite
> #
> library(lavaan);
> modelData <-read.csv(file=..., header = TRUE);
> model<-"
> DVmale ~ X1male + X2male + X1female + X2female
> DVfemale ~ X1female+ X2female + X1male + X2male
> DVmale ~~ 0.1528028*DVmale
> DVfemale ~~ 0.2171088*DVfemale
> DVmale ~~ DVfemale
> ";
> result<-sem(model, data=modelData, estimator = "ML", fixed.x=FALSE, missing = "FIML");
> summary(result, fit.measures=TRUE, standardized=TRUE)

Your mode constrains the error terms of regressions, not measurement errors. Doing the measurement error correction does not change the DF of the model. The proper way to correct for measurement error is to add a latent variable whose error variance is fixed to a known value

LDVmale ~ X1male + X2male + X1female + X2female
LDVfemale ~ X1female+ X2female + X1male + X2male

LDVmale ~= DVmale
DVmale ~~ 0.1528028*DVmale

LDVfemale ~= DVfemale
DVfemale ~~ 0.2171088*DVfemale

LDVmale ~~ LDVfemale

But it is not clear why would want to use the kind of model that you are using. If you use alpha as a reliability measure, you must assume that a factor model holds for the indicators. Because you must make this assumption, it would be more straightforward (and rigorous) to just specify LDVfemale and LDVmale as factors in the model without creating composites of their indicators. Errors in variables models do not do much to help with sample size issues.

Mikko

>
> When I run the model using Approach 1, most of the regression paths are significant and in the theoretically predicted direction. If I were not applying error corrections at all, I would have fully saturated model, and therefore (trivially) perfect fit. But the addition of the error corrections is adding 2 df to the model, putting me in a small-df situation for estimating model fit. Following Kenny (http://davidakenny.net/kkc/c7/c7.htm), I am essentially using the APIM as a "regression hack" to account for the fact that scores for male and female members of couples are non-independent - model fit per se is not my primary concern, but rather the significance and direction of the regression coefficients. > #

> #

> DVmale_Latent ~ X1male + X2male + X1female + X2female
> DVfemale_Latent ~ X1female + X2female + X1male + X2male

> DVfemale_Observed ~~ .1571883984*DVfemale_Observed
> DVmaleLatent ~~ DVfemaleLatent
> ";
> result<-sem(model, data=modelData, estimator = "ML", fixed.x=FALSE, missing = "FIML");
> summary(result, fit.measures=TRUE, standardized=TRUE)
>

Although I have read a good bit about error corrections in SEM, I am a bit confused whether I am applying them appropriately in lavaan, as well as the more general question of which of the two approaches above is correct (or maybe neither of them)? I'd appreciate any insights.
>

Dear all,

Thanks to Yves Rosseel, we found the main reason for the above mentioned warning.

We have too few clusters (only 6 sites) for an analysis whereby the clusters are considered as random component. For the same reason we were not able to properly model our data with the lavaan.survey package.

A possible solution would be to either model a multigroup SEM. Another option could be to model a fixed effect SEM with forest site as a compound variable (i.e. made up of five binary variable, 5 = n-1) or try to include latitude and longitude as continuous variables. Afterwards one need to check for spatial autocorrelation in the residuals to see if this was sufficient to remove the non-independence.

messages.subject: Casewise residuals for latent variable models
messages.subject_clean: Casewise residuals for latent variable models
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

We are trying to model a SEM with observations nested within sites (6 different forests, with in every forest 27 to 43 observations = 202 observations in total). I try to model the interaction between trees, leaf litter quality, soil quality and earthworm components. I hereby hypothesise a positive feedback loop between the different components of our model.

Both multilevel modelling and a lavaan.survey approach do not work for our data as we have to few clusters (=6 forests) (see my previous post “two-level SEM”). Also a multigroup SEM does not work (model can’t converge) as the model has to estimate too much parameters in relation to the number of observations.

Instead, we tried to model our data with a fixed effect SEM including latitude and longitude to correct for spatial autocorrelation. In order to verify whether including latitude and longitude is sufficient to remove the non-independence of our hierarchical data we need to check for spatial autocorrelation in the residuals (fitted response variables-observed).

We extracted the casewise residuals with residuals(fit_modlist, "casewise"), as all response variables in our SEM are latent variables (inferred from open issue #44). The result, however, are very small residual values (e.g. -4.4e-16). It looks like these values are not correct and wonder what we did wrong.

This is our model syntax:

fit_modlist<- '

#latent

Soil =~ pH0_10

worm =~ WormB_McCune

litter =~ litterPCA1

humus =~ humusPCOA1

#regressions

Soil   ~  humus + Lat + Long

worm   ~  Soil + litter + Lat + Long

humus  ~  worm + litter + Lat + Long

'

Any advice to solve this would be helpful. Many Thanks!

messages.body_plain:
Neitehr of these ideas is an exact answer to your question:
     Your "measurement model" simply equates 4 observed variables with 4 "latent variables"--the latter and identical with the former. The only source of lack of fit is the same as for a path model among observed variables--the missing paths between predictors and dependent variables. If those missing paths are largely consistent with the data, then residuals may be generally small.
     If you use the sem or cfa function to estimate the model, then by default the "latent variables" will be on the same scale as the observed variables. If the observed variables take on small values, then the residuals may also be very small, even if there are substantial discrepancies between model and data.

messages.subject_clean: Casewise residuals for latent variable models
messages.body_plain:
Hans (?),
Two thoughts spinning off of Ed's comments:

1. As I understand it, the casewise residuals predict the latent variable scores from the observed variables and then predict the observed variables from the latent variable scores using only the measurement model.  Your measurement model must be restricted in ways not shown  in the model code given that you have only one indicator per latent variable.  So, I am not sure what you should expect from casewise residuals in your application.  It is not clear to me that the casewise residuals can help you evaluate the structural part of the model.  Long and Lat are involved only in the structural part of the model.

2. Entering Lat and Long as linear effects assumes a constant linear effect for N/S location and a constant linear effect for E/W location.  That probably does not capture the kinds of patterns you have in mind.  I envision a cluster centered a a particular x,y coordinate and diffusing in every direction from that point.  Even if you include a linear interaction between Lat and Long, this still assumes a monotinic linear effect of, say, Lat on the effect of Long.  So, I wonder if you would not be better off to simply dummy code Forest and treat that as a fixed effect.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

messages.subject: Re: CFA with Likert-type indicators
messages.body_plain:
> I would like you to confirm that the correct analysis must consider indicators of type "ordered".

They are ordered, so the "correct" analysis is the one that takes that fact into account.  There is some evidence that results are nearly unbiased when treating 5-category ordered indicators as continuous (http://psych.colorado.edu/~willcutt/pdfs/Rhemtulla_2012.pdf), but you need 7 categories if the thresholds are asymmetric.  So you are probably better off treating them as ordered.

> Moreover, as I understand, lavaan automatically selects the suitable estimator and other stuff; nevertheless, do you recommend to write additional options in the functions 1. - 3.?

If your variables are of class "ordered" in the data.frame, or if you tell lavaan they are ordered, lavaan will appropriately use DWLS estimation with robust SEs and test statistic.

http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/cat.html

messages.subject: Re: issues with a two-stage cfa model from the semTools package
messages.subject_clean: issues with a two-stage cfa model from the semTools package
messages.body_plain:
> I can't seem to make it adopt robust hubert white standard errors.

The robust SEs are applied in the first stage, when the saturated model is fit to the raw incomplete data.  In the second stage, only the model parameters are estimated, by fitting the target model to the model-implied covariance matrix and mean vector from Stage 1.  That is why there is no way to apply robust SEs in Stage 2.  The information about nonnormality from the robust corrections derived in Stage 1 are used to correct the naïve SEs in Stage 2.

> does it give me reliable output?

No, you should not be applying lavaan methods to the individual lavaan objects from Stages 1 or 2.  See the class?twostage help page for available methods to apply to the output of twostage().  In other words, don't use summary(out1@target), use summary(out1).  The fit statistic (no indices yet) is available from anova(out1), not fitMeasures(out1@target), but the scaled statistic is too high.  Haven't been able to locate a bug or miscalculation yet, but when comparing the scaled statistic to the residual-based one (only available when data are assumed normal) and to FIML output, it is obvious that the residual-based statistic is executed correctly, whereas the scaled statistic is inflated (because the estimated scaling factor is too small).

Terrence D. Jorgensen

Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.body_plain:
> The p-values the reviewer is asking about would be more along the lines of regression p-values.

The p values for each parameter's Wald z test is a two-sided test, assuming the null hypothesized population value = 0.  If you want to conduct a directional hypothesis test, you can check the sign of the parameter and, if it is direction of the alternative hypothesis, divide the p value by 2.

messages.body_plain:
This startup output bothers me:

[Workspace restored from /Users/Katherina/.RData]

It looks like you are using RStudio, which has default settings to automatically save your workspace when you shutdown RStudio, then load it automatically when you start RStudio in the same directory.  That can have unintended negative consequences, such as loading the same namespaces that were loaded before (sometimes preventing proper re-installation, or loading an irrelevant package that also has a coef method that is competing with semTools for some reason).

Click on Tools --> Global options... , and in the General tab, do 2 things:
uncheck the box that says "Restore .RData into workspace at startup
Choose "Never" in the drop-down menu next to "Save workspace to .RData on exit"
Then shut down and restart RStudio.  You can delete the (probably hidden) .RData file from your directory, if you feel like it -- it serves no purpose unless you want to save something specific, which should be in your R scripts rather than something automatic that RStudio does without asking you first.

When you have restarted RStudio, run sessionInfo() first thing to make sure nothing is attached except the base packages:

> attached base packages:
> [1] stats     graphics  grDevices utils     datasets  methods   base

Then run library(semTools), which will automatically load lavaan.  There should be no need to re-install the latest versions of software that are already installed.  After running your script in this fresh session, do you still get the error message about not finding coef()?

messages.subject: Re: Significance for Modification Indices
messages.body_plain:
> So how would I be able to get a p-value for a given modification index?

The "mi" column is the chi-squared value, so you can find its probability using pchisq().  As Ed said, they are 1-df tests, so the critical  value using alpha = 5% is 3.84 (without adjusting for multiple testing).  You should control for the number of tests you are doing:

library(lavaan)
example(modindices)
MIs <- modindices(fit)
MIs$pvalue <- pchisq(MIs$mi, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE) # naïve p value
## possibly save a subset of rows you are interested in, then...
MIs$bonf.p <- p.adjust(MIs$pvalue, method = "bonferroni") # keeps familywise Type I errors below alpha level
MIs$FDR.p <- p.adjust(MIs$pvalue, method = "fdr") # keeps false discovery rate below alpha level
MIs

A smarter, less overly conservative way to do so would be to consider ahead of time which modification indices you would be willing to free for theoretically justifiable reasons.  Then you can save that subset of rows of the modindices() output, and the adjustments to p values will not be so conservative as to lose all power.  Forethought about your tests is also a way to prevent inadvertently letting the data make decisions for you, which has been shown to consistently fail to lead researchers to a better-fitting model that also generalizes to new samples from the same population.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

1  1  NA NA

model <-'

'

fit <- cfa(model, data = Y,std.lv <http://std.lv>=T,missing='fiml',ordered=c("Q1","Q2","Q3","Q4")
summary(fit,fit.measures=TRUE, standardized=TRUE, rsquare=TRUE)

item from 1930s): you should have had more forms with anchor items
among them.

messages.subject: Re: polychoric correlation with alternate forms
messages.body_plain:
You also cannot use FIML with categorical outcomes in lavaan.  ML assumes normal data, although continuous is sufficient because there are nonnormality corrections to SEs and tests (not sufficient for binary outcomes because those relationships will be underestimated, if the latent-response assumption holds).  So multiple imputation would be necessary to handle the missingness.

> I wonder if there might be some workaround? Maybe treat this as a 2 group analysis--one group received form A, another group received form B? There are no shared items; but people were randomly assigned to test form.

Well, sufficient auxiliary information might be able to bail you out here, assuming strong correlations both with and among the latent responses underlying your binary items.  If there are other observed variables that are associated with both {Q1, Q2} and {Q3, Q4}, then an association between those forms might inferred indirectly, at least within reasonable bounds.  For instance, if A is correlated .7 with B and .8 with C, then there are certain logical boundaries for the B-C correlation, beyond which the correlation matrix would be NPD (impossible to observe).  Here is a Cudeck (200) paper that discusses this in the continuous case with covariances among items not jointly observed:

https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007%2FBF02296344?LI=true

Not sure how pivotal the linearity and normality assumptions are, i.e., it might not work as well when imputing binary data because it won't draw on the simplifying normality assumption -- but I imagine the same principle applies to some degree.  But if it does not capture sufficient information to fit a factor model to those 4 items, that should be reflected in your pooled point and SE estimates.  Worth a try.  Check out the ?cfa.mi help page in the semTools package for help; there's a categorical example at the bottom.  Might want to download the development versions if you decide to use it:

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/lavaan/Mz__T8_DlUM/gvyXApiIAgAJ

Good luck,

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: polychoric correlation with alternate forms
messages.body_plain:
Chris,
You options may also depend upon the nature of the two forms.  If your alternate forms are parallel only in the classical sense, same mean and error variance, then you have 60 variables and Terrence's suggestion might offer your best option.  If your alternative forms are parallel in the modern sense of following the same test specification so that there is a one-to-one pairing of items from the two forms, then you can treat this as a two-group measurement invariance analysis by reconfiguring the data to have 30 variables plus a group/form variable instead of 60.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

messages.subject: Measurement Invariance
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am having a problem regarding measurement invariance. More specifically, I tested measurement invariance between group of gender. Following the output from that analysis:

Measurement invariance models:

Model 1 : fit.configural
Model 2 : fit.loadings
Model 3 : fit.intercepts
Model 4 : fit.means

Scaled Chi Square Difference Test (method = "satorra.bentler.2001")

                Df   AIC   BIC  Chisq Chisq diff Df diff Pr(>Chisq)
fit.configural  86 14505 14775 220.46
fit.loadings    95 14527 14761 260.06     13.579       9     0.1381
fit.intercepts 104 14522 14720 273.05     14.405       9     0.1086
fit.means      106 14552 14743 307.60                  2

According to results above, there should be a configural invariance, metric invariance, scalar invariance since all chi-squares do not significantly differ.

However, looking at output below, the results seem to be inconsistent with ones above.

Fit measures:

               cfi.scaled rmsea.scaled cfi.scaled.delta rmsea.scaled.delta
fit.configural      0.970        0.022               NA                 NA
fit.loadings        0.949        0.027            0.020              0.005
fit.intercepts      0.938        0.028            0.011              0.001
fit.means           0.878        0.040            0.061              0.011

You can see in the section of "Fit measures" and you will notice that cfi.scaled.delta are all greater than .01, which is the cutpoint recommended to attain measurement invariance.

Could you please so kind help me explain these results?

Thank you very much in advance,

Best regards,

Torres

messages.subject_clean: Problem with -> Scaled Chi Square Difference Test (method = "satorra.bentler.2001")
messages.body_plain:
> It reports the unscaled Chisq and the unscaled Chisq difference... Shouldn't it report the scaled ones?

Yes, it reports the unscaled chi-squared statistic for each model, because that is how the test is performed.  But it performs that adjustment on the test statistic (i.e., the difference between models' naïve chi-squared values), so the difference statistic in the output is the scaled one.  The scaled overall test statistic for each model is irrelevant -- that is not the test you are performing when you compare models.

Terrence D. Jorgensen

Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: R2 for composite variables
messages.body_plain:
R2 = 1 is the result of forcing residual variance to 0.

You used the "formative" operator here:
Filter <~1*Hmax + LMA
(which is not a good idea--it's buggy)
If Filter is a simple composite of Hmax and LMA, then there is nothing else in Filter to explain--it is an exact function of Hmax and LMA.

I believe that what you want is to use this line:
  Filter ~NH4 + GWC
to run a regression with NH4 and GWC predicting the composite of Hmax and LMA. But SEM doesn't work ike that. There is only 1 equation per dependent variable. So the method somehow combines your 2 lines of syntax into 1 equation.
Look at your output--what is the actual formula for Filter, according to the output?
--Ed Rigdon

messages.subject: Re: R2 for composite variables
messages.body_plain:
Well, that's confusing. It does make it seem like there are two separate equations--when there *can't* be, because this is a factor-based package. My guess is that the mathematical reality is that Filter is a composite of 4 variables with 0 residual variance, which is not what you intend.
     lavaan estimates a factor-based model. In such a model, each unobserved variable is defined by covariances among its dependents, subject to constraints like the zero residual variance constraint. Your composite, Filter, has many dependents--it predicts DF, mean.D, density, biomass and gain. These variables have other dependents, some of which compose Filter, so the situation is not simple.
      You can try relaxing the 0 residual variance assumption, but that would then make Filter a common factor defined by its dependents and predicted by (not composed of) Hmax, LMA, NH4 and GWC. Such a model may or may not be statistically identified, but it still won't get you what you want, which is an "optimally" weighted composite of Hmax and LMA predicted by NH4 and GWC.
     What you might consider, if you want to continue with factor-based methods, is to form your own composite of Hmax and LMA outside the  model, and then use that composite as a variable inside the model--leaving out Hmax and LMA. You don't use them anywhere else in the model, so it seems the loss would be small. You might (easily) create a range of composites, using different weights, to see if it makes any difference. If sample size is small and the components are highly correlated, any difference will be small, possibly swallowed up in residual variance.
     An alternative would be to use some composite-based method to estimate your model, but some people object to composite-based approaches.
--Ed Rigdon

messages.subject: Re: differential item functioning
messages.body_plain:
Global tests are incredibly difficult to calibrate; this is a general problem, not just one of DIF. The only way around it, if you insist on using a global test to verify any assumptions, is choosing a lower significance threshold. A rule of thumb might be along the lines of 5/n or (1-power)/2. Such rules aren't widely discussed in the literature, but prespecifying such a rule and its rationale is acceptable and reproducible. A different approach, with N=4,000, might be to develop a prediction model and calibrate out-of-sample predictive accuracy allowing for fitted values with do and do not allow for DIF.

I hope it is okay to post this in this group and would be very thankful for any help.

Petra

messages.subject: Odd Suggestion in Modification Indices
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

We have been attempting to construct an unconditional autoregressive latent trajectory model with structured residuals (ALT-SR as depicted by Figure 7 in Curran et al., 2014 <https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4067471/>). Below is the code to our model for two variables, “rail” and “dep” observed at four time points. Note that the rail variable intentionally does not include a slope factor because our basic, univariate LGC suggested as much. Further, we have constrained dep’s latent structure to zero because we had several issues with negative and non-positive definite variances and covariances.

modelaltxy <- '
# growth curve rail
# intercept only
i =~ 1*rail1 + 1*rail2 + 1*rail3 + 1*rail4
i ~ 1
i ~~ i

rail1 ~~ rail1
rail2 ~~ rail2
rail3 ~~ rail3
rail4 ~~ rail4

#autoregressive paths for derailment
rail2~a1*rail1
rail3~a2*rail2
rail4~a3*rail3

# growth curve dep
# s2 and i2 variances constrained to zero
i2 =~ 1*dep1 + 1*dep2 + 1*dep3 + 1*dep4
i2 ~ 1
i2 ~~ 0*i2
s2 =~ 0*dep1 + 1*dep2 + 2*dep3 + 3*dep4
s2 ~ 1
s2 ~~ 0*s2
dep1 ~~ dep1
dep2 ~~ dep2
dep3 ~~ dep3
dep4 ~~ dep4

# autoregressive components dep
dep2 ~ b1*dep1
dep3 ~ b2*dep2
dep4 ~ b3*dep3

#cross-sectional covariances
dep1 ~~ rail1
dep2 ~~ rail2
dep3 ~~ rail3
dep4 ~~ rail4

# latent intercept and slope covariances
# except s2s and i2s to zero.
i2~~0*s2
i~~0*s2
i~~0*i2

# crossed effects
dep2 ~ rail1
dep3 ~ rail2
dep4 ~ rail3
rail2 ~ dep1
rail3 ~ dep2
rail4 ~ dep3
'

fit.altxy <- lavaan(modelaltxy, data = ceswide, mimic = "Mplus", missing = "fiml")
summary(fit.altxy,fit.measures=TRUE)
modindices(fit.altxy)

The model does not fit as well as we would like. In attempting to respecify the model, you can see that we called the modification indices. As such, we’re left with two questions. First, how is rail1~1 even an option? Second, if we were to free this parameter, what would that even mean?

Thank you for any insights,
Kaylin

messages.subject: Re: Odd Suggestion in Modification Indices
messages.body_plain:
This is a general SEM question and not a lavaan question, so you should try semnet. However, it is illogical to use i2 and s2 as predictors when their variances are 0. If i2 and s2 were dependent, then the statements would be constraining *residual* variances to 0, which could possibly make sense. Remember, a regression coefficient is basically a covariance divided by variance of predictor, so a 0 variance predictor is impossible. I suggest you retreat to a plausible model and THEN think about modifications--or retreat even further and reexamine the whole research process. Sorry.

> i am under the impression that you have either thresholds or intercepts, but not both. could you expand on that a bit?

You typically only estimate one or the other (but that is always not necessary), but they are still both part of the model.  The latent responses are assumed continuous/normal, so they have a mean/intercept, and the observed variables are discrete,  so they have thresholds that correspond to how large the latent response needs to be before the observed response is assigned to a higher category.

messages.body_plain:
Kaylin,
  I agree with Ed that you might be better off posting to SEMNET for a question that is not lavaan specific.  However, here are two thoughts.

  Ed poses an interesting puzzle.  Perhaps the answer is that c(x,y)/var(x) is an estimator not a definition and the estimator does not apply when var(x) = 0.  After all, the intercept in an OLS regression model can be thought of as a weight for a constant predictor with a value of 1.

  As I understand your model, i is a baseline value for Rail at time 1 and the model relies on the autoregressive effects and cross-lagged effects to account for any mean differences across time.  Suppose that these affects cannot account for such differences.  Then Rain2 through Rain4 might pull i away from the mean of Rain1.  That would create a large residual for the mean of Rain1 which might account for the modification index.  If the means of Rain2 through Rain4 are all similar, then adding an extra threshold for Rain1 might make sense.  If they differ linearly with time, then perhaps you need to add and s parameter as you did for the other outcome variable.  I would suggest taking a close look at the residuals, sample statistics, and implied statistics to try to sort that out.

  Perhaps it would also be helpful to use lavaan or a spread sheet to compute the sample statistics from your model with all the parameters specified.  Some trial and error with different parameter values might provide some insight into the impact of various parameters on the means.

Keith
------------------------

messages.body_plain:
If a variable vv (observed or factor) is dependent, then the reference

vv

applies to the residual variance of vv rather than to vv itself.

So if vv is dependent on some other variable, then

vv~~zz

(where zz is some other variable) enables a free covariance between vv and zz or rht residual of zz, if zz is also dependent.

However, if zz is dependent on vv, as in:

zz ~ vv

Then alowing a free residual covariance violates a basic assumption of OLS regression and may make the model "not identified," so that it cannot be estimated. Read about "instrumental variables" in structural equations if you want to learn about how to estimate such a coefficient.

Mahima,
Your basic strategy sounds sensible to me.  The usual practice is to fit a sequence of models to better identify the sources of the differences.  Any introduction to measurement invariance will fill in the details for you.

One thing that I notice is that you have 8 latent factors but fewer than 8(8+1)/2 variances and covariances for the latent factors.  Check to make sure that you are not unintentionally constraining some of these to zero.

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am trying to test the following model with three mediators in a half-longitudinal design:

Dependent Variable: t2_learn
Independent Variable: t1_eo_mast
Mediators: t1_lgo / t2_lgo, t1_emoreap / t2_emoreap, t1_meta / t2_meta
Controls: t1_sex, t1_intell, t1_env_host, t1_fam, t1_bus_course, t1_learn

The idea of the half-longitudinal design is that "a" (see Baron & Kenny, 1986) is predicted by
t2_mediator (lgo/ emoreap/ meta) ~ a*t1_eo_mast + t1_mediator + controls
and "b" by
t2_learn ~ b*t1_mediator (lgo/ emoreap/ meta) + t1_eo_mast + t1_learn + controls

Here is my sem:

mod1.ind <- "

# latent variable definitions
lt1_eo_mast =~ 0.849*t1_eo_mast
lt1_learn =~ 0.970*t1_learn
lt1_sex =~ 1*t1_sex
lt1_intell =~ 1*t1_intell
lt1_env_host =~ 0.866*t1_env_host
lt1_fam =~ 1*t1_fam
lt1_bus_course =~ 1*t1_bus_course
lt1_emocon =~ 0.889*t1_emocon
lt2_emocon =~ 0.812*t2_emocon
lt2_learn =~ 0.927*t2_learn
lt1_meta =~ 0.959*t1_meta
lt2_meta =~ 0.933*t2_meta
lt1_lgo =~ 0.843*t1_lgo
lt2_lgo =~ 0.860*t2_lgo

# regressions
lt2_learn ~ b1*lt1_emocon + b2*lt1_lgo + b3*lt1_meta + lt1_eo_mast + lt1_learn + lt1_sex + lt1_intell + lt1_env_host + lt1_fam + lt1_bus_course

lt2_emocon ~ a1*lt1_eo_mast + lt1_emocon + lt1_sex + lt1_intell + lt1_env_host + lt1_fam + lt1_bus_course
lt2_lgo ~ a2*lt1_eo_mast +  lt1_lgo + lt1_sex + lt1_intell + lt1_env_host + lt1_fam + lt1_bus_course
lt2_meta ~ a3*lt1_eo_mast + lt1_meta + lt1_sex + lt1_intell + lt1_env_host + lt1_fam + lt1_bus_course

# indirect effects

indirekt1 := a1*b1
indirekt2 := a2*b2
indirekt3 := a3*b3

total:=indirekt1 + indirekt2 + indirekt3

# (co)variances & residual variances

t1_eo_mast ~~ 0.179*t1_eo_mast
t1_learn ~~ 0.060*t1_learn
t1_sex ~~ 0*t1_sex
t1_intell ~~ 0*t1_intell
t1_env_host ~~ 0.416*t1_env_host
t1_fam ~~ 0*t1_fam

t1_meta ~~ 0.049*t1_meta
t2_meta ~~ 0.035*t2_meta
t1_lgo ~~ 0.345*t1_lgo
t2_lgo ~~ 0.362*t2_lgo
"

As I am new to SEM and I have not found an SEM doing both - half-longitudinal and multiple mediators - I want to check with you, if this is correct?? Do I need to fix any parameters? The model is identified, however I have seen in other SEM certain variables fixed to 0. Any feedback would be great. Thanks!!!

messages.body_plain:
Hi Everyone,

I'm new to lavann and currently trying to use the growth function to model some longitudinal data. I am examining whether cognitive functioning changes in line with disease progression. Disease progression is measures by a disease staging system on an ordinal 1-4 scale.

So I'm modelling cognition over our four time points, and adding the disease stage as a time-varying covariate. However, I want to determine whether the effect of disease stage on cognition is linear or quadratic. I understand that to do so for time would be this:

model <- '
# intercept
i =~ 1*Time1 + 1*Time2 + 1*Time3 + 1*Time4
# slope 1
s1 =~ 0*Time1 + 1*Time2 + 2*Time3 + 3*Time4
# slope 2
s2 =~ 0*Time1 + 1*Time2 + 4*Time3 + 9*Time4
'

model <- '
  # intercept and slope with fixed coefficients
    i =~ 1*t1 + 1*t2 + 1*t3 + 1*t4
    s1 =~ 0*t1 + 1*t2 + 2*t3 + 3*t4
    s2 =~ 0*t1 + 1*t2 + 4*t2 + 9*t4
  # regressions
    i ~ x1 + x2
    s ~ x1 + x2
  # time-varying covariates
    t1 ~ c1
    t2 ~ c2
    t3 ~ c3
    t4 ~ c4
'
fit <- growth(model, data = Demo.growth)
summary(fit)

But how do you apply a quadratic function to a TVC (or even, can you)? Would it be appropriate to square disease stage as a new variable and enter it as a second TVC?

model <- '
  # intercept and slope with fixed coefficients
    i =~ 1*t1 + 1*t2 + 1*t3 + 1*t4
    s1 =~ 0*t1 + 1*t2 + 2*t3 + 3*t4

  # regressions
    i ~ x1 + x2
    s ~ x1 + x2
  # time-varying covariates
    t1 ~ c1+c1^2
    t2 ~ c2+c2^2
    t3 ~ c3+c3^2
    t4 ~ c4+c4^2
'
fit <- growth(model, data = Demo.growth)
summary(fit)

Thanks in advance!

messages.body_plain:
Mahima,
I went back to look at your code and I think that I partly misunderstood your question (perhaps confusing it with another thread).

If I understand you correctly now, you are not doing measurement invarance but are instead interested in testing the hypothesis that the same mediation model applies in both cities with no differences in parameters across cities.

You still might find it useful to test measurement invarance with a CFA first so that if you find invarance overall you can better determine the source.  Also, invariant regression parameters may not be meaningful without measurement invariance.

You have two options for constraining parameters to equality across your two cities.  You can do this manually by giving the parameter the same name in both cities.

WFE ~ c('a','a')*RCW

However, given that you have a large number of parameters, you may find it helpful to use the group.equal() parameter to impose these constraints on many parameters all at once.  See the Multiple Groups page in the lavaan tutorial for a list of key words and other details.

In your output, check to confirm that you have estimated residual variances for every latent variable (e.g., WFE ~~ WFE) and unique variances for every indicator (e.g., DK3 ~~ DK3).  You appear to be relying on convenience functions to add these to your model.

Keith

John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus

I think you should render the 4-level ordinal disease stage variable into 3 dummy variables, one set of 3 for each point in time. Then it might make sense to impose a pattern of loadings consistent with a quadratic effect (1--4--9) across the three indicators of disease stage at each time point. But you might prefer to leave those paths free and examine the result path estimates for evidence of a quadratic pattern. You may have to leave some of the dummies out, where its values are constants at a certain time point (say, the highest disease stage at the earliest time point).

messages.body_plain:
> # indirect effects
>
> indirekt1 := a1*b1
> indirekt2 := a2*b2
> indirekt3 := a3*b3

Looks correct.

> total := indirekt1 + indirekt2 + indirekt3

This may not be the total effect of t1_eo_mast on t2_learn.  To make sure you have identified all possible indirect paths, you can inspect powers of the Beta matrix.

fit <- sem(mod1.ind, data, ...)
(B <- lavInspect(fit, "est")$beta) # direct effects
(B %*% B) # 2-parameter indirect paths
(B %*% B %*% B) # 3-parameter indirect paths, should be all zeros for a half-longitudinal model

Each nonzero value in (products of) Beta matrices indicate (in)direct path, with the predictor variable represented in the column and the (ultimate) outcome variable represented in the row.

> Do I need to fix any parameters?

Not unless that is a hypothesis you need to test.

messages.subject: Re: Conﬁrmatory Factor Analysis with ordinal data
messages.subject_clean: Conﬁrmatory Factor Analysis with ordinal data
messages.body_plain:
> Bill Revelle's "polychoric" function from the "psych" package is able to by using the correction for continuity (i.e., argument "correct"). I thought that the lavaan argument "zero.add" did the same. What is "zero.add" doing if not correcting for zero cell frequencies by replacing the zero frequency with a small decimal (e.g., .01)?

That addresses zeros in 2-way contingency tables between outcome/indicator variables, the same thing Bill does in the psych package.  You are describing a different problem, which is zeros in a 2-way contingency table between an outcome/indicator and the grouping variable.  In other words, a zero cell for the 7-level variable means you only observed 6 categories, so there is no way for the software to get information about how frequent the 7th category is endorsed.  That means there is no way to estimate the 6th threshold, so the polychoric correlation (in that group) has to be estimated by treating it as a 6-category indicator.  If the numbers of observed response categories differ across groups, there is no logical automatic way for the software to link 5 thresholds from one group to 6 thresholds in another group.  You would have to do that manually, assuming you can give different models to different groups.  Most people, however, solve this problem by collapsing categories so that all groups have the same number of observed categories, and thus estimated thresholds.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

> I get an error and negative variances.

If there was an error, you would not be able to inspect model output because the model fitting would have failed.  Do you mean there is a warning message, simply letting you know there are negative variances?

> How do I know if this is a problem with (1) my model or (2) my data, and second, how do I fix this?

I have responded to lots of posts about investigating NPD matrices / Heywood cases, you can search the lavaan forum for them.  Basically, read this to test whether your out-of-bounds estimate is "significantly" out of bounds, or whether the CI also includes plausible values (which would indicate you cannot rule out sampling error as the cause):

http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/0049124112442138

If you can rule out sampling error as the cause, and your chi-squared is significant, then model misfit is probably the cause.  If you you cannot rule out sampling error as the cause, and your model fits fine, then it is most certainly just sampling error.  If you cannot rule out sampling error as the cause, but your model also does not fit, then the results are ambiguous -- could be either sampling error or misfit that caused the inadmissible value.

Terrence D. Jorgensen

Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

Thanks for your thoughts Terrence. That makes sense; however, I am doing a total sample CFA (i.e., no multi-group analysis). With a "single-group" CFA model, it was my understanding lavaan would just drop any categories with zero *univariate* frequency cells; for example, if one cell has no observed frequencies, then reduce a 7-level category variable to a 6-level categorical variable with only 5 (rather than 6) estimated thresholds. I now understand (thank you Terrence) that the "zero.add" argument in lavaan is for zero *bivariate* frequency cells in a 2-way contingency table.

I played around with the lavaan arguments and found something interesting. If I input my full dataset with missing values into lavaan and specify missing = "listwise", I get the following error:  lavaan ERROR: some categories of variable `GQ1.1' are empty in group 1; frequencies are [1 15 32 82 184 0]. But, if I create a listwise datatset on my own (i.e., using the base R function "na.omit") and then input that listwise deleted dataset into lavaan, the model runs. I am not sure if it is something unique to my data or something with the lavaan package code. Here is the syntax I ran:

# Full dataset with missing values
fit <- lavaan(model = conf, data = dat, estimator = "WLSMV", std.lv <http://std.lv> = T,
+               zero.add = c(.001,.001), missing = "listwise",
+               ordered = c("GQ1.1","GQ2.1","GQ4.1","GQ5.1",
+                                  "GQ1.4","GQ2.4","GQ4.4","GQ5.4",
+                                  "GQ1.5","GQ2.5","GQ4.5r","GQ5.5r"))
Error in lav_samplestats_step1(Y = Data, ov.names = ov.names, ov.types = ov.types,  :

  lavaan ERROR: some categories of variable `GQ1.1' are empty in group 1; frequencies are [1 15 32 82 184 0]

# Listwise deletion dataset with no missing values
dat.listwise <- na.omit(dat[,c("GQ1.1","GQ2.1","GQ4.1","GQ5.1",
                                             "GQ1.4","GQ2.4","GQ4.4","GQ5.4",
                                             "GQ1.5","GQ2.5","GQ4.5r","GQ5.5r")])
fit <- lavaan(model = conf, data = dat.listwise, estimator = "WLSMV", std.lv <http://std.lv> = T,
+               zero.add = c(.001,.001),
+               ordered = c("GQ1.1","GQ2.1","GQ4.1","GQ5.1",
+                                  "GQ1.4","GQ2.4","GQ4.4","GQ5.4",
+                                  "GQ1.5","GQ2.5","GQ4.5r","GQ5.5r"))

On Saturday, August 26, 2017 at 6:39:33 AM UTC-4, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> > Bill Revelle's "polychoric" function from the "psych" package is able to by using the correction for continuity (i.e., argument "correct"). I thought that the lavaan argument "zero.add" did the same. What is "zero.add" doing if not correcting for zero cell frequencies by replacing the zero frequency with a small decimal (e.g., .01)?
>
> That addresses zeros in 2-way contingency tables between outcome/indicator variables, the same thing Bill does in the psych package.  You are describing a different problem, which is zeros in a 2-way contingency table between an outcome/indicator and the grouping variable.  In other words, a zero cell for the 7-level variable means you only observed 6 categories, so there is no way for the software to get information about how frequent the 7th category is endorsed.  That means there is no way to estimate the 6th threshold, so the polychoric correlation (in that group) has to be estimated by treating it as a 6-category indicator.  If the numbers of observed response categories differ across groups, there is no logical automatic way for the software to link 5 thresholds from one group to 6 thresholds in another group.  You would have to do that manually, assuming you can give different models to different groups.  Most people, however, solve this problem by collapsing categories so that all groups have the same number of observed categories, and thus estimated thresholds.
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: multicore option for fitting a model in lavaan
messages.subject_clean: multicore option for fitting a model in lavaan
messages.body_plain:
What independent task do you expect each core to perform?  ML estimation is an iterative process that requires knowledge of the previous iteration to know how to iterate forward, so that task cannot be farmed out to independent processes that don't communicate with each other.

If you were fitting this model to a series of data sets (e.g., in a simulation or multiple imputations), you could use the parallel options in the lavaanList() function.  If you were bootstrapping, the bootstrapLavaan() function has parallel options (same situation: the model is fit independently to a bunch of different data sets, so that can be done on different cores).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject_clean: lavaan WARNING: some estimated ov variances are negative
messages.body_plain:
> For the record, the model more or less made sense given the pattern of the data (sig positive latent slope, which matches overwhelminingly with the visual inspection of the data).

Did you look at individual growth plots for each individual, with either splines/lowess curves or linear and quadratic fitted lines, to see whether the linearity assumption was appropriate?  Model fit might not be your concern here, but estimation problems are more likely to occur when models do not fit well, so it is still worth investigating.  Here is a textbook example for generating empirical growth plots in R (see Figure 2.3 for a useful one to check the linearity assumption):

https://stats.idre.ucla.edu/r/examples/alda/r-applied-longitudinal-data-analysis-ch-2/

> I did try constraining the residual variances to be equal, but that now forces a non-positive-definite latent variable covariance matrix (slope-intercept correlation @ 1.37) and negative eigenvalues. Further, the pattern of the results seems strange.
>
> Thus, I'm at a loss. The model is predetermined, so there is not much else I can do. Is it possible to identify the source of the problem?

If you already had NPD issues, fitting a more-constrained error structure will probably not help, as you saw.  Did you inspect correlation residuals to see whether the model fails to capture some observed relationships?

resid(fit, type = "cor")

If some variables are more correlated than the model accounts for, you may need to specify an error covariance structure (e.g., autoregressive, allowing adjacent time points to be correlated, which you can also constrain to equality for all adjacent pairs if the time points are equally spaced), instead of assuming independent errors by default (one of the big criticisms of the SEM approach to growth modeling).  Curren & Bollen's autoregressive latent trajectory (ALT) model attempts to address this problem, although in my experience it often has estimation difficulties -- perhaps because a simple autoregressive structure won't always be appropriate.

> ONE other thing: the observed variable is non-normal, but that shouldn't matter? (Count data).

You can adjust SEs and test statistics for nonnormality by requesting a robust estimator (see ?lavOptions help page, the se, test, and estimator arguments).  If your mean count is at least 20, the normal distribution is often a good approximation of Poisson.  If your counts are lower (e.g., mean of 10 or lower), then you probably have predicted values that are negative, which makes no sense for counts.  Since this is such a basic univariate growth curve, you might want to consider using the MLM framework instead of SEM.  In the lme4 package, the glmer() function allows you to specify family = poisson(link = "log"), a more appropriate model for counts that are not overwhelmingly large and approximately normal.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

My first post here.  Apologies in advance, advice about good introductory texts may be needed, I'll come back to that.

I'm trying to replicate analyses in Nelson, T. D., B. S. Aylward, and J. R. Rausch. 2011. ‘Dynamic P-Technique for Modeling Patterns of Data: Applications to Pediatric Psychology Research’. Journal of Pediatric Psychology 36 (9): 959–68. doi:10.1093/jpepsy/jsr023 which has supplementary material with the following MPlus syntax:

TITLE:            Dynamic P-Technique Example for JPP

DATA:            FILE IS C:\PTechExampNegMood.dat;

VARIABLE:  NAMES ARE Pain PainLag Mood1 Mood1Lag

Mood2 Mood2Lag Mood3 Mood3Lag Mood4 Mood4Lag

Mood5 Mood5Lag;

MODEL:         Mood BY Mood1 (1);

        Mood BY Mood2 (2);

        Mood BY Mood3 (3);

        Mood BY Mood4 (4);

        Mood BY Mood5 (5);

        MoodLag BY Mood1Lag (1);

        MoodLag BY Mood2Lag (2);

        MoodLag BY Mood3Lag (3);

        MoodLag BY Mood4Lag (4);

        MoodLag BY Mood5Lag (5);

        Pain ON PainLag MoodLag;

        Mood ON PainLag MoodLag;

OUTPUT: Standardized;

And runs with the data (dat.csv attached) that is also in the supplementary material to the paper.  The Lavaan code I've used is:

require(lavaan)

dat <- read.csv(dat.csv)

colnames(dat) <- c("Pain",
                   "PainLag",
                   "Mood1",
                   "Mood1Lag",
                   "Mood2",
                   "Mood2Lag",
                   "Mood3",
                   "Mood3Lag",
                   "Mood4",
                   "Mood4Lag",
                   "Mood5",
                   "Mood5Lag")

model3 <- 'mood1 =~ Mood1
                  + Mood2
                  + Mood3
                  + Mood4
                  + Mood5
              moodLag =~ Mood1Lag
                     + Mood2Lag
                     + Mood3Lag
                     + Mood4Lag
                     + Mood5Lag
              mood1 ~ moodLag + PainLag
              Pain ~ moodLag + PainLag
              PainLag ~~ moodLag
              Pain ~~ mood1'
finalFit3 <- cfa(model3,data=dat)
summary(finalFit3,fit.measures=TRUE,standardized=TRUE)

The output shown in the paper, which clearly simplifies that MPlus model is:

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-lNEWEzPMNpc/WaVsDw2hQGI/AAAAAAAAACE/9Ae5c4D1qRwyGFXI331E4dRrDd5EkmcMQCLcBGAs/s1600/Figure3.png>
What I'm getting from Lavaan is:

lavaan (0.5-23.1097) converged normally after  32 iterations
##
##   Number of observations                           199
##
##   Estimator                                         ML
##   Minimum Function Test Statistic               52.688
##   Degrees of freedom                                50
##   P-value (Chi-square)                           0.371

and this:

Regressions:
##                    Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)   Std.lv  Std.all
##   mood1 ~
##     moodLag           0.435    0.086    5.042    0.000    0.427    0.427
##     PainLag           0.078    0.022    3.482    0.000    0.112    0.251
##   Pain ~
##     moodLag           0.867    0.227    3.826    0.000    0.594    0.264
##     PainLag           0.437    0.061    7.104    0.000    0.437    0.436
##
## Covariances:
##                    Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)   Std.lv  Std.all
##   moodLag ~~
##     PainLag           0.344    0.123    2.783    0.005    0.502    0.223
##  .mood1 ~~
##    .Pain             -0.089    0.091   -0.979    0.327   -0.152   -0.081

Two things strike me as very odd here:
1) the df in paper from MPlus are said to by 54 and mine from Lavaan says 50.  I find myself
counting things off and getting to 50 not 54 but I know that I haven't dealt with models with
two latents and two observed predictors with no measurement model attached to them so I wonder
if I'm miscounting that and misspecifying the Lavaan.
2) the "diagonal" regressions from PainLag to mood1 and from moodLag to Pain in my output seem
to be reversed compared with those in that figure from the published paper.

Can anyone see things here that will help me?!

Now it's a very long time since I last used SEM software regularly (15+ years) and then
it was just CFA with the then versions of LISREL and AMOS so I know I need to do some
serious (re)learning.  I love R and have used it for pretty much all my stats work in the last 12+ years
and I like the look of Lavaan.  I've had a look at OpenMx and SEM but for the moment haven't worked
out how to specify this model in them.  I have access to modern AMOS and I can specify the
mood measurement models in its visual model creator but it's refusing to let me put in the structural
regressions and covariances.

I'm currently working in a university with no maths or stats departments and I'm probably one of the

If anyone can recommend contemporary introductory reading for these sorts of SEM models, particularly

ones focused on Lavaan (or the other R SEM systems), I'd be interested to hear that general advice as

TIA,

Chris

messages.body_plain:
The first thing that you are missing is the labels from the original Mplus syntax. The "(1)" through "(5)" in the Mplus syntax are labels, and when the same labels are used again, this imposes equality constraints on the parameters so labeled. These equality constraints are missing from your lavaan code.
     In lavaan syntax, you label parameters this way:
mood1 =~ a*Mood1 + b*Mood2 + ...
[[I think it is bad practice to have different variables differentiated only by uppercase / lowercase on the first letter, but that's just me]]
Labels must be alphabetical in lavaan--the numeric labels from the ecxample would be taken as fixed values assigned to the parameters. But a - e will work as well as 1 - 5.
     Imposing these 5 equality constraints, by using the same labels for the Mood and Moodlag indicators, will save you 4 DF. (The first indicator for Mood and for Moodlag will have its loading fixed to 1 by default, anyway, so they are already "equal," even without these constraints.)
     If you want a text on using lavaan, Alex Beaujean has one:

https://www.amazon.com/Latent-Variable-Modeling-Using-Step/dp/1848726996/ref=sr_1_fkmr0_1?ie=UTF8&qid=1504016041&sr=8-1-fkmr0&keywords=beaujean+lavaan

messages.subject: Re: Is it right to fix both the factor variance and one factor loading?
messages.subject_clean: Is it right to fix both the factor variance and one factor loading?
messages.body_plain:
Spring,
  Your model does not violate any assumptions of SEM.  However, it is likely to raise eyebrows because it is atypical.  You need to be certain that you are doing what you intend to do and to be sensitive to the atypicality when you report your results.

  In a perfect world, we might specify fixed values for all of the parameters in our model.  This would provide a highly testable hypothesis with maximal degrees of freedom.

  In practice, we typically cannot specify such precise hypotheses and instead test classes of models that vary by the values of free parameters.  To do this, we give up degrees of freedom and our hypothesis becomes less testable.

  When one crosses the line from imposing only identification constraints to imposing testable constraints, one narrows the class of models being tested.  This narrowing becomes part of the hypothesis.  If one can do that deliberately, great.  If one stumbles into it by accident, it may not be what one wants to do.

  When you fix both the loading and the factor variance in your example, you are imposing a testable constraint, not just an identification constraint.  If one has reason prior to looking at the data to believe that this constraint should hold, one can test it in this fashion.  Lacking such a prediction, it is less clear what one might accomplish with such a constraint.  Sometimes there are things that one can do with SEM that do not match up with any useful research strategy or scientific inference.  Imposing such a constraint after looking at the data might fall into the latter category.

  You might find it helpful to think about this in terms of a multiple-group analysis rather than a generalization from past data to present data.  The constraint that you are imposing is generally less interpretable than the kinds of constraints imposed in a measurement invariance study (equal loadings, equal intercepts, equal unique variances).  You are fixing the amount (not ratio of) explained variance in the reference item.  So, reading an introduction to measurement invariance might help to clarify the issues for you.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

messages.subject: Re: Help with confidence intervals for standardised regression coefficients
messages.subject_clean: Help with confidence intervals for standardised regression coefficients
messages.body_plain:
What Terrence said, in terms of methodology, is approximately true.
Instead of saying "unbiased", he should have said, "asymptotic". Very
few things are technically unbiased in statistics; the estimate of the
mean is when we are talking about i.i.d. data, and Horvitz-Thompson
survey estimator of the totals is when we are talking about data with
no nonresponse. Everything else is biased, period. Estimates and
standard errors that we get in SEM are biased, biased, biased, biased.
You may get an unbiased estimate of the means and the covariance
matrix, and then you twist them and screw them and stretch them and
reverse them with nonlinear maximization and the computations that the
standard errors require on top of that. (Read Browne 1984 to get a
feeling of just how complex the computations are.)

There are two main issues involved. First, the standard errors for
standardized coefficients are obtained through the delta method, and
with all the nonlinearities that are involved with that, the promised
land of asymptotia is pushed a little bit further away. Any
nonlinearity introduces or exacerbates small sample biases, and
introduces or blows up higher order moments like skewness and kurtosis
of the sampling distributions. Take a log of a positively distributed
variable, and the mean of the logs is not equal to the log of the mean
(read up on the lognormal distribution). What the delta method says is
that as the sampling distribution get tighter around the population
value (which we hope to achieve with larger sample sizes), the
variance of the nonlinear transformation gets tighter, as well, in
some predictable fashion. However, this is only an approximation --
and as an approximation, by Murphy's law, it is usually biased down,
making the standard errors anticonservative. Note that the standard
errors for unstandardized coefficients are themselves obtained by the
delta method approximations, and as such are less reliable than say
the standard errors for the item means (as if anybody is interested in
that trivia). So unstandardized standard errors aren't that great to
begin with, but by convoluting things and producing standardized
coefficients, you make things even less great.

The second issue is that most analytical derivations (have to) assume
that the model is correctly specified. When it isn't, things may get
iffy. If the model is not correctly specified, then you may end up
dividing your coefficient by a wrong quantity. In a more subtle way,
when the SEM model is incorrect, ADF/WLS standard errors are too
small. They are not necessarily disastrously small, but enough to get
worried about (in my simulations, the CIs had something like upper 80%
coverage; in some disastrous examples in other areas of statistics, I
have seen simulated 20% actual coverage).

Terrence points to the possibility of transforming the unstandardized
CIs, or by using likelihood profiles. These are good ideas -- but then
again the likelihood profile mostly makes sense with the model is
exactly right, and you have a multivariate normal distribution to deal
with. With non-normal data, you don't have that luxury.

-- Stas Kolenikov, PhD, PStat (ASA, SSC)  @StatStas
-- Senior Scientist, Abt Associates @AbtDataScience
-- Program Chair (2018), Survey Research Methods Section of the
American Statistical Association
-- Opinions stated in this email are mine only, and do not reflect the
position of my employer
-- http://stas.kolenikov.name

On Mon, Apr 17, 2017 at 8:55 AM, Terrence Jorgensen
<tjorge...@gmail.com> wrote:
>> Terrence (or anyone else), what's the reason for using unstandardized
>> coefficients for inferences about a null hypothesis instead of standardized
>> coefficients?
>
>
> Historically, I think this had something to do with the SEs not being
> trustworthy when analyzing correlation matrices instead of covariance
> matrices (at least in certain models without constraining residual variances
> to be 1 - explained variance).
>
> http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.105.2.317
>
> Since null (nil) hypotheses of zero are interpreted the same way for
> unstandardized and standardized parameters (no effect or relationship), the
> same hypothesis can be tested using the unstandardized estimate's test
> statistic or CI.  And the standardized point estimate is used for
> interpretation, if we don't want reference to an arbitrarily set scale for
> latent common factors.  Of course, we need to be careful about interpreting
> standardized effect sizes that way because we use sample estimates of
> variances to standardize, rather than any known population variance, and
> variances are also affected by design issues (e.g., how homogeneous is the
> sampling frame?), so standardized effect sizes are often not comparable
> across studies anyway. Here's some interesting reading on the subject:
>
> http://dx.doi.org/10.1348/000712608X377117
> http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/a0028086
>
> Of course nowadays, it has been worked out how to calculate unbiased SEs for
> standardized solutions, but I don't think that means unstandardized
> solutions should be ignored.  A host of more seasoned SEM veterans on SEMNET
> might have more to say about this tradition, if you want to try posting this
> question there:
>
> http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html
>
>> It would seem strange to me to report the p-value for the unstandardized
>> coefficient together with the estimate and confidence interval for the
>> standardized coefficient.
>
>
> Well, according to the APA manual, we are expected to report an estimate
> along with a test statistic, df (if applicable), p value, CI for the
> estimate, and a standardized measure of effect size.  As Dr. Bonett pointed
> out, it would be naïve not to report a CI along with the point estimate of a
> standardized effect size, because those are just as susceptible to sampling
> variability as unstandardized estimates.  But I am unsure whether
> normal-theory CIs calculated from SEs for standardized estimates are
> appropriate, or whether unstandardized confidence limits should be
> transformed -- maybe the latter is wrong if the sampling variability of
> estimates used to standardize also need to be considered in the
> transformation.  Likelihood profile CIs for standardized estimates would be
> great...  Anyway, I'd love to see literature on this.  Again, SEMNET might
> be a good place to ask about this, in case someone has already investigated
> the issue.
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of
> Amsterdam

On 08/30/2017 06:52 PM, NewInMediation wrote:

Yes, you can.

> fit.p16a18c24 <-
> sem(p16a18c24,data=m,missing="fiml",se="bootstrap",ordered="MyOutcome")
> Error in lav_options_set(opt) : use (D)WLS estimator for bootstrap

(note, "MyOutcome" should be "myOutcome")

When at least one observed variable is categorical, the default
estimator is WLSMV, which implied estimator = "DWLS", se = "robust", and
test = "scaled.shifted".

So to use the bootstrap, you need to specify the estimator as "DWLS":

fit.p16a18c24 <- sem(p16a18c24, data = m, se = "bootstrap", ordered =
"myOutcome", estimator = "DWLS", verbose = TRUE)

Yves.

> > So to use the bootstrap, you need to specify the estimator as "DWLS":

> > fit.p16a18c24 <- sem(p16a18c24, data = m, se = "bootstrap", ordered =
> > "myOutcome", estimator = "DWLS", verbose = TRUE)
> >
